docs.text: tensor-optix tensor-optix is a training loop framework with statistical convergence control, online hyperparameter optimisation, and an optional neuroevolution subsystem for dynamic policy topology. It runs your agent against a pipeline (a Gymnasium environment, a live data stream, or a PyTorch Dataset ), maintains a separate validation signal, and manages four loop states - ACTIVE , COOLING , DORMANT , and watchdog shutdown - using statistical trend detection rather than a fixed patience counter or step budget. Hyperparameters are tuned online every episode via SPSA gradient estimates. Checkpointing and rollback are driven by the validation signal, never the noisy training score. On DORMANT , a MetaController decides whether to spawn a policy variant, prune the ensemble, or stop. Why Most RL training scripts hard-code a step budget, a learning rate, and a hope that both were right. tensor-optix replaces that with: Convergence detection via a corrected t-test on the smoothed score slope plus lag-1 autocorrelation - not "stop after N episodes without improvement." Online hyperparameter tuning via SPSA (and three other optimizers, auto-routed by an AdaptiveOptimizer ) - no separate sweep needed for most params. Validation-only checkpointing - the agent that gets restored at the end of training is the one that generalises, not the one that overfit the training window hardest. An optional neuroevolution subsystem - a policy whose topology (neurons, edges, recurrent connections) grows and prunes itself live during training, gated by three independent statistical signals. Where to go New to the library? Start at Installation and the Quickstart . Want to understand the loop before using it? Read Concepts . Already know what you want to do? Jump to a Guide . Looking up a specific class or function? See the API Reference . Algorithms included 15 agents ship out of the box, all implementing the same six-method BaseAgent interface and interchangeable with RLOptimizer : Framework Agents PyTorch PPO, Gaussian PPO, Recurrent PPO, DQN, Rainbow DQN, SAC, TD3 TensorFlow PPO, Gaussian PPO, DQN, SAC, TD3 JAX / Flax PPO Bring your own algorithm by implementing BaseAgent - see Write a custom agent . Learning-to-Learn Engine An optional layer on top that learns across training runs rather than within one: a structured experiment ledger, concurrent trial scheduling, cross-task transfer with a conservative abstention gate, a closed grammar for discovering better training procedures, and a recommend-only live adaptive runtime that never auto-promotes a change. See the Learning-to-Learn Engine guide .

docs.text: Contributing Getting started git clone https://github.com/sup3rus3r/tensor-optix cd tensor-optix pip install -e ".[dev]" Development rules These rules exist to keep the library clean and portable. No algorithm-specific code in core/ . PPO, DQN, SAC, etc. must never be referenced in core/ or loop_controller.py . Gymnasium API only. Use (obs, info) = env.reset() and (obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info) = env.step() . Never use the legacy done flag. HyperparamSet.params is opaque. Core code must never read or hardcode specific key names. Separation of concerns. The optimizer tunes hyperparameters. PolicyManager evolves models. Do not mix these. Framework code stays in adapters. TF/Torch/JAX-specific code belongs in adapters/<framework>/ , not scattered through core. Running tests pytest tests/ All tests must pass before a PR is merged. Tests that require TensorFlow use pytest.importorskip("tensorflow") and are skipped automatically if TF is unavailable. Submitting changes Fork the repo and create a branch from main . Make your changes. Add or update tests to cover your changes. Ensure pytest tests/ passes. Open a pull request with a clear description of what changed and why. Reporting bugs Use the bug report issue template. Include a minimal reproducible example where possible. Suggesting features Use the feature request issue template. Frame requests in terms of use cases, not implementation - explain what problem you're solving.

docs.text: Concepts Two cores, not one Everything below describes the RL core : LoopController , BaseAgent , episodes. There is a second, separate ML core ( tensor_optix.ml_core ) for supervised/unsupervised training: Trainer , BaseMLModel , epochs and batches. It is not a mode of the RL loop. An ML training epoch is not an RL episode. The older Optimizer(model, dataset) path treats a training epoch as a fake RL episode (see ML support ); ml_core does not. The two cores share the same lower-level, algorithm-agnostic pieces ( CheckpointRegistry , BackoffScheduler , SPSAOptimizer ) but expose different contracts on top. See Train an ML model . The five abstractions LoopController (wrapped by RLOptimizer and, more simply, Optimizer ) coordinates five things through abstract interfaces. It has no knowledge of TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, PPO, DQN, or SAC - only these contracts: Abstraction Role BaseAgent act() , learn() , hyperparams, save/load weights - the only thing the loop calls into BasePipeline Produces EpisodeData - a Gymnasium env, a live stream, or a Dataset BaseEvaluator Scores an episode into a single primary_score (higher is always better) BaseOptimizer Proposes new hyperparameters from score history LoopCallback Hooks into loop events (improvement, plateau, dormant, degradation, ...) Any algorithm - PPO, DQN, SAC, CMA-ES, a custom evolutionary method - is usable by the loop as long as it implements BaseAgent 's six methods. See Write a custom agent . Loop states ACTIVE → COOLING → DORMANT → (watchdog shutdown | policy spawn) ↑________________| (on improvement or degradation) ACTIVE - the score is improving or it's early in training. COOLING - plateau_threshold consecutive non-improving evals. Only windows in which at least one episode finished count as evals, and nothing counts until min_completed_episodes_before_dormant (default 10) episodes have finished. DORMANT - dormant_threshold consecutive non-improving evals. By default the loop stops here and restores the best checkpoint. With a PolicyManagerCallback attached, DORMANT instead triggers a spawn/prune/stop decision. Transitions are not point-to-point score comparisons. BackoffScheduler fits a linear trend over the most recent trend_window scores and compares the slope against an adaptive floor ( noise_k × the standard deviation of the recent scores around their own linear trend, capped at 50% of |best_score| ) - the noise estimate is detrended so that steady improvement is not mistaken for noise. A single unlucky episode in an otherwise-improving run does not look like a collapse, and a single lucky episode in an otherwise-flat run does not look like genuine progress. Checkpointing is validation-only When a val_pipeline is configured, primary_score is the validation score, not the training score. The training score can keep climbing while validation degrades - that's overfitting, and the loop is built to act on it rather than reward it. run() always restores the best known checkpoint before returning, regardless of how the loop ended (convergence, stop() , or max_episodes ). Pass checkpoint_score_fn to drive checkpoint selection from an independent, deterministic external evaluation instead of the noisy training-window mean. By default, "best" is the single episode with the highest primary_score - a raw point comparison. That's fine most of the time, but a lucky episode (reward concentrated on one favorable step, not earned consistently) can score higher than anything a genuinely better policy produces later, and become a permanent, unbeatable "best." criteria_mode and checkpoint_confirmation (both opt-in, off by default) widen the measurement and require corroboration before trusting an improvement - see Avoiding unicorn checkpoints . On-policy vs. off-policy rollback BaseAgent.is_on_policy (default True ) tells the loop whether rollback is safe: On-policy (PPO, A2C) - each window is freshly generated by the current policy. Rolling back to a previous checkpoint is safe; the next window will be generated entirely by the restored policy. Off-policy (SAC, DQN, TD3) - a replay buffer holds experience from all past policies. Rolling back weights without clearing the buffer means the agent immediately trains on stale, mismatched experience, corrupting Bellman targets. LoopController skips weight rollback for off-policy agents even when rollback_on_degradation=True . Online vs. trial-level hyperparameter tuning Two layers, meant to compose: Online ( BaseOptimizer subclasses: SPSA, Momentum, Backoff, PBT, Adaptive) - adapt hyperparameters within a single run, every episode, by probing and measuring score deltas. Good at tracking a non-stationary landscape; bad at exploring broadly. Trial-level ( TrialOrchestrator ) - runs N independent short trials via Optuna TPE before the main run, then warm-starts the full run from the best trial's weights and config. Good at finding the right region of hyperparameter space; too slow to run continuously. See Tune hyperparameters online and Run trial-level search . DiagnosticController vs. the optimizer SPSA-style optimizers are deliberately slow and blind to internals - they see only the score, and a meaningful update takes several episodes. That's fine for global search but useless against an acute failure happening right now : a loss spike, entropy collapse, a KL-divergence blowup, or an exhausted DQN exploration budget. DiagnosticController reads train_diagnostics from agent.learn() every episode and applies an immediate, single-parameter correction when a threshold is crossed - independent of, and faster than, the episode-level optimizer. Ensembles and evolution PolicyManager is deliberately separate from the optimizer: the optimizer tunes hyperparameters, PolicyManager evolves models . On DORMANT , MetaController reads the generalization gap (level and slope) and the validation improvement rate, then issues SPAWN , PRUNE , STOP , or NO_OP . See Ensembles and policy evolution .

docs.text: Installation tensor-optix requires Python ≥ 3.11. # Core loop only, no algorithm implementations pip install tensor-optix # PyTorch algorithms pip install tensor-optix[torch] # TensorFlow algorithms pip install tensor-optix[tensorflow] # JAX/Flax pip install tensor-optix[jax] # Neuroevo subsystem (requires torch) pip install tensor-optix[neuroevo] # GPU (Linux/WSL2, CUDA 12.8) pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 pip install tensor-optix[torch] # All frameworks and environment extras pip install tensor-optix[all] Optional extras Extra Adds [box2d] Box2D Gymnasium environments (LunarLander, BipedalWalker) [atari] Atari environments via ale-py [mujoco] MuJoCo environments [wandb] WandbCallback [tensorboard] TensorBoardCallback [onnx] export_onnx() on Torch agents [dev] pytest, ruff, mypy, black, twine - for contributing Core dependencies The base install pulls in: gymnasium[box2d] >= 1.0.0 numpy >= 1.24.0 matplotlib >= 3.7.0 optuna >= 3.0.0 (used by TrialOrchestrator ) pyyaml >= 6.0 (used by the YAML config loader) torch >= 2.11.0 The core loop, PolicyManager , and all ensemble/evolution logic have no framework dependency beyond this - TensorFlow and JAX are opt-in via their respective extras. CLI Installing the package registers a tensor-optix command: tensor-optix train config.yaml seed=42 agent.learning_rate=1e-3 tensor-optix validate config.yaml See Configure via YAML / CLI .

docs.text: Quickstart Discrete action space (CartPole) import gymnasium as gym from tensor_optix import make_agent, Optimizer env = gym.make("CartPole-v1") agent = make_agent(env) # -> TorchPPOAgent (discrete default) opt = Optimizer(agent, env) opt.run() make_agent inspects env.action_space and env.observation_space and returns a fully constructed agent with sensible default hyperparameters and network sizes. Optimizer wraps RLOptimizer with auto-computed window_size , automatic SPSA hyperparameter tuning (when the agent declares default_param_bounds ), and neuroevo callback wiring. Continuous action space env = gym.make("LunarLanderContinuous-v3") agent = make_agent(env) # -> TorchSACAgent (continuous default) agent = make_agent(env, deterministic=True) # -> TorchTD3Agent opt = Optimizer(agent, env) opt.run() Choosing an algorithm explicitly agent = make_agent("DQN", env) agent = make_agent("RAINBOW", env) agent = make_agent("SAC", env, framework="tf") Parallel environments opt = Optimizer(agent, lambda: gym.make("CartPole-v1"), n_envs=8) opt.run() When n_envs > 1 , pass env as a zero-arg callable (or a list of callables) rather than a constructed environment - each subprocess/sync worker needs to build its own instance. What you get back opt.run() opt.best_snapshot # PolicySnapshot: best weights + EvalMetrics + HyperparamSet When run() returns - whether because of convergence, a manual stop() , or max_episodes - the agent's weights are always the best known checkpoint, not the last one trained. See Concepts for why. Next steps Concepts - understand the loop states and why checkpointing is validation-driven. Train an RL agent - the full RLOptimizer constructor, validation pipelines, and callbacks. Build a neuroevo agent - policies that grow and prune their own topology.

docs.text: Configure via YAML / CLI For reproducible runs and parameter sweeps without touching Python code, define a training run as a YAML file. Config schema # config.yaml env: CartPole-v1 algorithm: TorchPPOAgent seed: 42 agent: learning_rate: 3e-4 clip_ratio: 0.2 gamma: 0.99 n_epochs: 10 minibatch_size: 64 optimizer: max_episodes: 300 verbose: true checkpoint_dir: ./checkpoints Required keys: env (a Gymnasium env ID string) and algorithm (one of TorchPPOAgent , TorchSACAgent , TorchTD3Agent , TorchDQNAgent , TorchGaussianPPOAgent , TorchRecurrentPPOAgent , TFPPOAgent , TFSACAgent , TFTDDAgent , TFDQNAgent , TFGaussianPPOAgent ). Optional keys: framework (inferred from the algorithm name prefix if omitted), deterministic , pipeline ( "BatchPipeline" ; "LivePipeline" is only usable when the env object exposes a stream() data source, which Gymnasium envs do not - build live pipelines in Python), window_size , hidden_sizes . algorithm must be buildable for the env's action space - see Algorithm resolution . The agent and optimizer sub-dicts are forwarded verbatim - every YAML key maps 1:1 to a constructor kwarg, with no hidden defaults. Running from the CLI tensor-optix train config.yaml seed=42 agent.learning_rate=1e-3 tensor-optix validate config.yaml CLI overrides use dotted-key notation and take precedence over the file. Precedence order: defaults < config file < CLI overrides . validate parses and checks the config without running training - useful in CI to catch a typo'd algorithm name or missing required key before launching a job. It exits 0 on success, 1 on error. Loading config from Python from tensor_optix.config import load_config, build_agent_from_config, build_pipeline_from_config, build_optimizer_from_config cfg = load_config("config.yaml", overrides=["seed=42", "agent.learning_rate=1e-3"]) agent, hyperparams = build_agent_from_config(cfg) pipeline = build_pipeline_from_config(cfg) optimizer = build_optimizer_from_config(cfg, agent, pipeline) optimizer.run() apply_overrides(config_dict, overrides) and config_to_dict(cfg) are also exported for programmatic config manipulation - e.g. writing a sweep script that generates many config dicts and calls apply_overrides per trial. Override values are YAML-parsed so true , 1e-3 , and [64,64] all deserialize correctly. A float() fallback coerces strings that look numeric (e.g. PyYAML 1.1 doesn't auto-parse bare scientific notation like 1e-3 without special-casing it). Reference Full schema and function signatures: Config / CLI reference .

docs.text: Write a custom agent The loop never inspects an agent's internals - it calls exactly six methods. Any algorithm at all (a custom evolutionary method, CMA-ES, an algorithm that doesn't exist yet) is usable as long as it implements BaseAgent : from tensor_optix import BaseAgent from tensor_optix.core.types import EpisodeData, HyperparamSet class MyAgent(BaseAgent): def act(self, observation): """Given an observation, return an action. Must be fast - hot path.""" ... def learn(self, episode_data: EpisodeData) -> dict: """ Update weights given a completed episode's data. Return a dict of training diagnostics (loss, entropy, ...) - may be empty. """ ... def get_hyperparams(self) -> HyperparamSet: ... def set_hyperparams(self, hyperparams: HyperparamSet) -> None: ... def save_weights(self, path: str) -> None: ... def load_weights(self, path: str) -> None: ... Declaring on-policy vs. off-policy class MyOffPolicyAgent(MyAgent): is_on_policy = False Off-policy agents (those with a replay buffer accumulating experience from past policies, like DQN/SAC/TD3) must override is_on_policy to False . LoopController skips weight rollback for off-policy agents even when rollback_on_degradation=True - restoring weights without clearing the buffer would immediately corrupt Bellman targets and drag the policy back down. The default is True . Enabling SPSA out of the box If your agent declares default_param_bounds and default_log_params as class attributes, RLOptimizer / Optimizer will build an SPSAOptimizer automatically without you having to construct one: class MyAgent(BaseAgent): default_param_bounds = { "learning_rate": (1e-5, 1e-2), "entropy_coef": (0.0, 0.1), } default_log_params = ["learning_rate"] HyperparamSet.params is treated as a fully opaque dict everywhere in core - never assume the optimizer or loop reads specific keys. Your agent's set_hyperparams() is solely responsible for knowing how to apply each key (e.g. updating an optimizer's learning rate group). Optional hooks def average_weights(self, paths: list) -> None: """SWA: θ_avg = mean of weights loaded from each path. Default: no-op.""" def perturb_weights(self, noise_scale: float) -> None: """θ_new = θ × (1 + noise_scale × ε). Used by PolicyManager spawning. Default: no-op.""" def export_onnx(self, path: str) -> None: """Export the actor network. Default: raises NotImplementedError.""" def teardown(self) -> None: """Release GPU memory / file handles. Called by PolicyManager.prune(). Default: no-op.""" Implement average_weights if you want CheckpointRegistry.load_ensemble() (stochastic weight averaging across top-k checkpoints) to work for your agent. Implement perturb_weights if you want PolicyManager.spawn_variant() 's weight-space mutation to actually touch your network rather than being a no-op. Architectural rules (if contributing upstream) From CONTRIBUTING.md : No algorithm-specific code in core/ - PPO, DQN, SAC, etc. must never be referenced there or in loop_controller.py . Gymnasium API only - (obs, info) = env.reset() , (obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info) = env.step() . Never the legacy done flag. HyperparamSet.params is opaque - core code must never read or hardcode specific key names. Separation of concerns - the optimizer tunes hyperparameters; PolicyManager evolves models. Don't mix these. Framework-specific code belongs in adapters/<framework>/ , not scattered through core. Reference BaseAgent reference , BaseOptimizer , BaseEvaluator , BasePipeline .

docs.text: Distributed training (IMPALA + V-trace) AsyncActorLearner implements IMPALA-style asynchronous actor-learner training. N actor subprocesses read weights from shared memory (lock-free) and collect trajectories; the learner dequeues trajectories, applies V-trace importance-sampling correction, and writes updated weights back to shared memory - actors see the new weights immediately, with no explicit broadcast step. from tensor_optix.distributed import AsyncActorLearner learner = AsyncActorLearner( actor=actor, critic=critic, optimizer=optimizer, env_factory=lambda: gym.make("ALE/Pong-v5"), n_actors=8, trajectory_len=64, ) stats = learner.run(max_steps=10_000_000) # stats["steps_per_second"] -> ~4x single-process throughput on CPU Why V-trace Actors run a policy μ that may lag behind the learner's current policy θ (staleness from async collection). The importance ratio ρ_t = π_θ(a_t|s_t) / π_μ(a_t|s_t) corrects for this mismatch, with two clips to control variance: ρ̄_t = min(ρ̄, ρ_t) - clips the IS weight applied to the TD error c̄_t = min(c̄, ρ_t) - clips the IS weight applied to the trace (controls the bias/variance tradeoff) With ρ̄ = c̄ = 1 and synchronous actors ( μ = θ ), V-trace reduces to standard on-policy GAE with λ = c̄ . See Espeholt et al. 2018 ("IMPALA"). Platform notes fork is used automatically on Linux (no pickling required - subprocess objects are inherited via os.fork() ); spawn is used on Windows/macOS, which requires env_factory to be picklable (a module-level function or functools.partial , not a lambda capturing a non-picklable closure). When to reach for this This is for environments where single-process throughput is the bottleneck and your policy/critic are plain nn.Module s with a discrete action space - Atari-scale problems, not small classic-control envs where VectorBatchPipeline (synchronous, in RLOptimizer ) is simpler and sufficient. AsyncActorLearner is a standalone training loop, not wired into RLOptimizer 's convergence/checkpoint/SPSA machinery - use it when you specifically need the throughput and are comfortable managing your own stopping condition via max_steps . docs.text: Ensembles and policy evolution PolicyManager runs as a loop callback and is responsible for model evolution - separate from the optimizer's job of tuning hyperparameters. On each DORMANT event, MetaController evaluates the generalization gap (level and slope) and the validation improvement rate, then issues one of SPAWN , PRUNE , or STOP . Spawned variants are cloned from the best checkpoint with perturbed hyperparameters and (optionally) perturbed weights. EnsembleAgent wraps all active variants behind the BaseAgent interface, combining their actions via weighted averaging. Minimal: rollback only from tensor_optix import PolicyManager pm = PolicyManager(registry) cb = pm.as_callback(agent) opt = RLOptimizer(..., callbacks=[cb]) With no agent_factory , DORMANT rolls back to the best checkpoint and otherwise leaves the loop's own convergence/stopping logic in control. Spawning variants pm = PolicyManager(registry, max_spawns=4) cb = pm.as_callback(agent, agent_factory=lambda: make_agent(env)) # zero-argument factory cb.set_stop_fn(opt.stop) opt.add_callback(cb) opt.run() Each DORMANT event with budget remaining spawns a variant (best checkpoint weights + perturbed hyperparameters and weights), the scheduler is reset to ACTIVE , and training continues. set_stop_fn should be set when spawning is enabled - when the spawn budget is exhausted, PolicyManagerCallback calls it to terminate the loop cleanly with the best-known weights already restored. With max_spawns=4 the run therefore passes through DORMANT five times: four spawns, then the stop. Letting MetaController decide Without a MetaController , PolicyManagerCallback spawns whenever budget allows. With one, the spawn/prune/stop decision is signal-driven: from tensor_optix import MetaController mc = MetaController(gap_threshold=0.2, gap_slope_threshold=0.02, improvement_threshold=0.01) cb = pm.as_callback(agent, agent_factory=lambda: make_agent(env), meta_controller=mc) cb.set_stop_fn(opt.stop) MetaController checks, in order: spawn budget exhausted → STOP ; generalization gap level too high → PRUNE ; gap actively widening (even if level is still tolerable) → PRUNE ; validation improvement too flat → SPAWN ; otherwise → NO_OP . This requires a val_pipeline for the gap signals to be meaningful. Building an ensemble manually from tensor_optix import EnsembleAgent pm = PolicyManager(registry) pm.add_agent(agent_a, weight=1.0) pm.add_agent(agent_b, weight=0.5) ensemble = EnsembleAgent(pm, primary_agent=agent_a) pipeline.set_agent(ensemble) opt = RLOptimizer(agent=ensemble, pipeline=pipeline, ...) With several members, EnsembleAgent.act() returns the combined output of PolicyManager.ensemble_action() - for discrete PPO members that is an averaged probability vector to sample/ argmax , not an action index - so a multi-member ensemble is primarily an inference-time construct (see the reference ). EnsembleAgent.learn() trains every registered agent on the same episode data - this is mathematically necessary; non-primary agents that don't update will drift away from the primary's action distribution as training progresses, degrading the ensemble. get_hyperparams / set_hyperparams / save_weights / load_weights all delegate to the primary agent only - it's the authoritative agent for checkpointing. Regime-conditional boosting Outside the spawn/prune pipeline, you can shift ensemble weight toward a specific agent based on detected regime: from tensor_optix.core import RegimeDetector detector = RegimeDetector() regime = detector.detect(metrics_history) pm.set_regime(regime) if regime == "volatile": pm.boost(agent_volatile, factor=2.0) Inspecting state import json print(json.dumps(pm.status(), indent=2)) # after training: print(json.dumps(pm.training_report(), indent=2)) PolicyManagerCallback also prints a human-readable training report to stdout automatically when the loop stops via budget exhaustion or a MetaController STOP decision. Reference Full method signatures: PolicyManager , MetaController , EnsembleAgent .

docs.text: Add exploration bonuses (RND) Random Network Distillation (RND) adds an intrinsic exploration reward to any pipeline without modifying the agent. Two small networks - a frozen random target and a trained predictor - both map observations to a fixed embedding space. Novel states produce high prediction error (high intrinsic reward); visited states are fitted well (low bonus). r_int(s) = ||f_θ(s) - g(s)||² (g frozen, f_θ trained) r_total = r_ext + η · r_int / σ(r_int) (intrinsic normalized per episode) Usage from tensor_optix.exploration.rnd import RNDPipeline from tensor_optix import RLOptimizer, BatchPipeline import gymnasium as gym base = BatchPipeline(env=gym.make("LunarLander-v2"), agent=agent, window_size=2048) pipeline = RNDPipeline(base, obs_dim=8, embedding_dim=64, eta=0.1) optimizer = RLOptimizer(agent=agent, pipeline=pipeline) optimizer.run() RNDPipeline wraps any BasePipeline . It intercepts each EpisodeData after collection and injects the intrinsic bonus into episode_data.rewards before the agent sees them, then trains the predictor network on the current batch's observations via plain SGD. Implementation is pure numpy (a minimal two-layer MLP) - no TF or Torch dependency, and RNDPipeline proxies any other attribute access through to the wrapped pipeline ( __getattr__ ), so it's a drop-in wrapper. Loop-controlled exploration schedule η (the intrinsic reward scale) is not static - LoopController calls pipeline.set_eta(...) automatically at state transitions, with zero cost for pipelines that don't implement set_eta : Event Effect on η improvement η *= 0.9 - pull back exploration while genuinely learning plateau ( COOLING ) η *= 1.5 , capped at 4 × η_base - push exploration harder when stuck DORMANT η = 0 - converged, stop injecting noise restart (after spawn) η = η_base - reset for the new policy variant This means you set the initial eta once and the loop adapts it automatically as training progresses - no manual exploration-decay schedule needed. Reference Constructor parameters and the _MLP internals: Exploration reference .

docs.text: Tune hyperparameters online All online optimizers operate in normalised [0, 1] parameter space and update every episode - no restarts required. They implement BaseOptimizer.suggest() and see only an opaque HyperparamSet plus score history; they never assume specific param names. Choosing an optimizer from tensor_optix.optimizers import SPSAOptimizer, AdaptiveOptimizer # SPSA: Rademacher perturbation vector, two-episode gradient estimate optimizer = SPSAOptimizer( param_bounds={"learning_rate": (1e-4, 3e-3), "clip_ratio": (0.1, 0.3)}, log_params={"learning_rate"}, # log-space normalisation for params spanning orders of magnitude ) # AdaptiveOptimizer: routes between SPSA, Momentum, Backoff, and PBT # based on lag-1 autocorrelation of the score stream and relative performance gap optimizer = AdaptiveOptimizer(param_bounds={...}) opt = RLOptimizer(agent=agent, pipeline=pipeline, optimizer=optimizer) Optimizer Routing condition SPSAOptimizer i.i.d. score noise, no autocorrelation structure - the default MomentumOptimizer Positive lag-1 autocorrelation (smooth landscape) BackoffOptimizer Negative lag-1 autocorrelation (oscillating landscape, sign-only updates) PBTOptimizer Score below 20th percentile of history (exploit checkpoint population) AdaptiveOptimizer Routes automatically based on the two signals above If you don't pass optimizer= at all, RLOptimizer builds an SPSAOptimizer from the agent's default_param_bounds / default_log_params class attributes automatically. Why SPSA by default SPSA updates all N bounded params in exactly 2 episodes regardless of N (one + probe, one − probe, then commit), versus BackoffOptimizer 's round-robin 2N episodes. For an agent with 3-5 tunable params that's a 3-5x speedup with an unbiased gradient estimate (Spall, 1992). Use AdaptiveOptimizer once you suspect the score landscape isn't i.i.d. - e.g. it's visibly oscillating between hyperparameter updates, or stuck below its own historical best. Suppressing false degradation during probes Every probing optimizer exposes is_probing ( True during a probe episode). LoopController checks this before firing degradation handling - a score drop caused by a deliberate finite-difference probe is not a policy collapse, and treating it as one would trigger unnecessary rollback and reset the convergence scheduler. Combining with DiagnosticController Online optimizers are slow by design - a meaningful SPSA update takes several episodes. For acute, single-episode failures (loss spikes, PPO entropy collapse, KL blowups, exhausted DQN epsilon), RLOptimizer always wires in a DiagnosticController that reacts immediately and independently. Tune its thresholds via the diag_* kwargs on RLOptimizer if the defaults don't suit your environment. See DiagnosticController reference . Reference Full algorithm details (math, parameters, routing logic) are in the Optimizers reference .

docs.text: Learning-to-Learn Engine Everything else in tensor-optix tunes one training run. The Learning-to-Learn Engine is a layer on top that learns across runs: it records every experiment with enough structure to compare reliably, lets you search and discover better training procedures, and — for a long-running deployed agent — continuously proposes evidence-based interventions for a human to review. It is built in six layers, each composing over the one before it, and each layer can be used on its own. No layer here uses generative AI or runs arbitrary generated code. Strategy discovery works over a small, closed set of hand-written typed operations, reconstructed only from a fixed registry — never eval / exec . 1. Experiment ledger The foundation every other layer reads from and writes to: a SQLite-backed ExperimentStore that records each trial's provenance (code revision, library versions, hostname), lifecycle state, and scores. from tensor_optix.ledger import ExperimentStore, ExperimentState, EvaluationStatus store = ExperimentStore("./experiments.sqlite3") record = store.create_experiment( task_env="CartPole-v1", algorithm="PPO", framework="torch", seed=0, checkpoint_dir="./ckpt", solve_threshold=475.0, ) store.start_experiment(record.experiment_id) store.record_progress(record.experiment_id, best_primary_score=480.0) store.finalize_experiment( record.experiment_id, state=ExperimentState.COMPLETED, evaluation_status=EvaluationStatus.VALIDATED, ) Every write is idempotent on experiment_id , and every method opens a short, single-statement transaction — nothing here holds a lock for the duration of training. The schema also carries three tables for strategy discovery (below): strategy_candidates , strategy_evaluations , strategy_registry . 2. Concurrent trial scheduler ConcurrentTrialScheduler runs multiple Optuna trials as real, isolated OS processes — the parent process is the sole owner of the Optuna Study and the ledger; workers never touch either directly, they just train and report scores back over a queue. from tensor_optix.scheduler import ConcurrentTrialScheduler scheduler = ConcurrentTrialScheduler( agent_factory=make_agent, pipeline_factory=make_pipeline, param_space={"learning_rate": ("log_float", 1e-4, 3e-3)}, n_trials=20, n_workers=4, trial_steps=50_000, ledger_store=store, task_env="CartPole-v1", algorithm="PPO", solve_threshold=475.0, ) best_params, best_score = scheduler.run() TrialOrchestrator (see Run trial-level search ) remains the simpler, correct tool when you don't need real process-level concurrency. 3. Baseline selection StrategySelector is the non-learned baseline: given a task's ledger history, it allocates a trial budget across competing methods by ranking their confidence-interval upper bound ( hi95 ), with a minimum exploration share for any method that hasn't been tried yet. from tensor_optix.selection import StrategySelector baseline = StrategySelector(store) decision = baseline.propose(task_env="CartPole-v1", methods=["TPESampler"], budget=10) print(decision.rationale) This is also the fallback every higher layer uses when it doesn't have enough evidence to do better. 4. Cross-task transfer (Nanonets) Tuning a new task from scratch throws away everything you already know about similar tasks. NanonetsSelector pools a source task's ledger evidence into a target task's estimate — but only after a conservative abstention gate confirms the source is actually comparable. The gate compares each task's scores normalized against its own solve threshold ( (score - threshold) / abs(threshold) ), not raw scores — comparing raw scores across tasks with different scales and signs (e.g. CartPole's ~0–500 against Acrobot's ~–500–0) is a real, demonstrated bug class, not a hypothetical one: a positive-scale task's data can numerically pass a percentile check against a negative-scale target purely by coincidence. A source passes only if its normalized median is at or above the target's own normalized 95th percentile. from tensor_optix.nanonets import NanonetsSelector selector = NanonetsSelector(store, source_task_envs=["Acrobot-v1"]) decision = selector.propose(task_env="CartPole-v1", methods=["TPESampler"], budget=10) # rationale states explicitly whether it pooled cross-task evidence or # fell back to the plain baseline because nothing passed the gate. The pooling itself (precision-weighted shrinkage, not a Gaussian Process or RGPE — deliberately simple, since multi-task GP correlation estimation is unreliable at the sample sizes real experiments produce) also normalizes before combining estimates, then de-normalizes back to the target's own raw units for display — pooling must happen in the same comparable space as the gate, or the same scale-mixing problem the gate exists to prevent resurfaces in the pooled number itself. source_task_envs is always supplied explicitly by the caller, never auto-discovered — for leave-one-task-out validation, the caller must already know which tasks are training sources versus held out. 5. Strategy discovery Hyperparameter search tunes values; strategy discovery searches procedures — a small, closed grammar of typed training-time interventions: Operation What it does LearningRateTrendOp Adjusts learning rate based on a measured score trend CheckpointRollbackOp Rolls back to the best checkpoint on a validation condition ExplorationBoundsOp Adjusts an algorithm's exploration knob ( entropy_coef , epsilon , TD3's target-smoothing noise) within bounds OptimizationMethodChoiceOp Switches which online tuning BaseOptimizer drives the run BudgetAllocationOp Reallocates ensemble budget toward a promising policy variant ScheduleChangeOp Overrides a schedule (DQN's epsilon_decay , RND's eta) PolicyVariantSelectionOp Boosts or prunes ensemble members by evidence Every operation wraps an already-existing mutation primitive ( agent.set_hyperparams , checkpoint_registry.load_best , PolicyManager.boost / prune ) as a LoopCallback . An operation that doesn't apply to a given agent (e.g. exploration bounds on TorchSACAgent , whose temperature is learned rather than a static hyperparameter) returns None from attach() and is silently skipped — self-exclusion, not a crash. from tensor_optix.strategy import LearningRateTrendOp, StrategyCandidate, StrategyTrialRunner op = LearningRateTrendOp(window=5, increase_factor=1.2, decrease_factor=0.5) candidate = StrategyCandidate.from_op(op) # content-hashed, versioned, serializable runner = StrategyTrialRunner( agent_factory=make_agent, pipeline_factory=make_pipeline, trial_steps=50_000, ledger_store=store, task_env="CartPole-v1", algorithm="PPO", solve_threshold=475.0, ) results = runner.run_candidate(candidate, seeds=[0, 1, 2]) Each seed runs a paired candidate-vs-baseline trial (same seed/task/budget, baseline has no strategy callback attached) so the comparison is honest, not candidate-vs-stale-history. Comparing and promoting compare_candidate gates on the pessimistic end of the outcome-delta confidence interval ( lo95 > margin ), not the mean, and hard-requires at least 3 distinct seeds before it can ever pass — the same conservative discipline as Nanonets' abstention gate, applied to "is this strategy's benefit trustworthy" instead of "is this source task comparable." PromotionPolicy checks six independent, inspectable criteria: from tensor_optix.strategy import PromotionPolicy, record_candidate_scope record_candidate_scope( store, candidate, train_task_envs=["CartPole-v1"], held_out_task_envs=["Acrobot-v1"], algorithms=["PPO"], frameworks=["torch"], budget_range_episodes=(50_000, 50_000), n_seeds_per_task=3, ) policy = PromotionPolicy(store, margin=5.0, min_seeds=3, min_held_out_tasks=1, approval_mode="human") verdict = policy.evaluate( candidate_id=candidate.candidate_id, train_task_envs=["CartPole-v1"], held_out_task_envs=["Acrobot-v1"], ) for name, passed in verdict.criteria.items(): print(name, passed) beats_baseline_margin , repeats_across_seeds , generalizes_held_out , meets_compute_constraints , and reproducible are all computed from ledger evidence. The sixth, human_reviewed , is different: in the default approval_mode="human" , evaluate() never sets it itself — it can only become True after a separate, explicit store.approve_strategy(candidate_id, reviewer=...) call made by an actual human. approval_mode="auto" exists for contexts that explicitly want full automation (it still requires all five automatable criteria to pass, and leaves a traceable reviewer="auto:PromotionPolicy" record — never a silent self-approval) — but the live adaptive runtime below never uses it. 6. Live adaptive runtime The final layer wires everything above into the proposal's observe → detect → propose → experiment → evaluate → recommend loop, run continuously against a long-running agent that stands in for a deployed model. from tensor_optix.runtime import LiveAdaptiveRuntime, RuntimeConfig, establish_baseline from tensor_optix.adapters.pytorch.torch_evaluator import TorchEvaluator baseline_id = establish_baseline( store, agent_factory=make_agent, pipeline_factory=make_pipeline, evaluator=TorchEvaluator(), task_env="CartPole-v1", algorithm="PPO", study_id="my_deployment", trial_steps=20_000, ) config = RuntimeConfig(task_env="CartPole-v1", algorithm="PPO", study_id="my_deployment", max_cycles=20) runtime = LiveAdaptiveRuntime(store, config, agent_factory=make_agent, pipeline_factory=make_pipeline) observations, recommendations = runtime.run() Each cycle: re-evaluates the deployed agent with a short, real, inference-only rollout (standing in for live traffic); feeds the score through a DeploymentObserver (a thin wrapper around the existing BackoffScheduler trend/degradation state machine — reused exactly as-is, not reimplemented); and, on degradation or a scheduled research cycle, consults NanonetsSelector to rank a fixed shortlist of strategy operations, runs the winners through StrategyTrialRunner , and issues a durable recommendation. The loop is recommend-only by construction, not by convention. PromotionPolicy is hardcoded inside the runtime with approval_mode="human" — there is no field on RuntimeConfig , no CLI flag, no environment variable that reaches that value. Recommendations are written as auditable ledger EventRecord s, never just a line of stdout that scrolls away. Nothing in the loop ever calls store.approve_strategy . Promoting a candidate to actually become the deployed baseline requires two separate, explicit actions outside the loop: from tensor_optix.runtime import promote_candidate_to_baseline # 1. A human reviews the recommendation and approves it. store.approve_strategy(candidate_id, reviewer="your-name") # 2. A separate, explicit call promotes the approved candidate's best weights. new_baseline_id = promote_candidate_to_baseline( store, candidate_id, reviewer="your-name", task_env="CartPole-v1", algorithm="PPO", study_id="my_deployment", ) promote_candidate_to_baseline refuses to act — raises ValueError — unless the candidate was already approved. It is never imported by any of the runtime's own loop modules. Honest results so far Real validation runs against this engine (CartPole-v1/Acrobot-v1/Pendulum-v1 with PPO and TD3) have mostly produced negative or inconclusive results at the tight, cheap probe budgets used so far — a few thousand training steps and 2–3 seeds, deliberately small to prove the mechanism works before spending a larger budget. Most candidate strategies and cross-task transfer attempts correctly triggered fallback or failed the promotion margin, rather than being accepted on noisy, low-powered evidence. That is the conservative gates working as designed, not a disappointing outcome to downplay — the proposal's own exit criteria explicitly accept "a documented negative result that informs the next research direction" as a legitimate deliverable, and this project treats it that way throughout. docs.text: Logging and dashboards Three callbacks ship out of the box, all subclasses of LoopCallback . Live terminal dashboard from tensor_optix.callbacks import RichDashboardCallback opt.add_callback(RichDashboardCallback( title="CartPole PPO", history=50, refresh_per_second=4, )) Requires pip install rich . The loop's hot path is never blocked - on_episode_end appends a lightweight event dict to a thread-safe deque and returns in well under a millisecond; a background daemon thread owns the rich.Live render loop and redraws at refresh_per_second Hz. Pass transient=True to erase the dashboard from the terminal when training stops, leaving a clean prompt. Weights & Biases from tensor_optix.callbacks import WandbCallback opt.add_callback(WandbCallback(project="my-project", name="run-1", tags=["ppo"])) Requires pip install wandb . Logs four signal groups every eval: score/* (primary, best, at-degradation), metrics/* (everything in EvalMetrics.metrics - algorithm diagnostics, reward stats, generalization_gap when a val pipeline is active), hyperparams/* (current values, logged on improvement and on every SPSA update), and spsa/step_magnitude (L2 norm of relative per-param SPSA changes - large during plateau exploration, small while actively improving). Plus binary events/* flags for improvement, plateau, convergence, and degradation. TensorBoard from tensor_optix.callbacks import TensorBoardCallback opt.add_callback(TensorBoardCallback(log_dir="./runs/cartpole")) Requires pip install torch (ships with torch.utils.tensorboard ) or pip install tensor-optix[tensorboard] . Logs the same signal groups as WandbCallback , using TensorBoard's / -separated scalar tag convention for grouped panels. Writing your own from tensor_optix import LoopCallback class MyLogger(LoopCallback): def on_improvement(self, snapshot): print(f"New best: {snapshot.eval_metrics.primary_score:.4f}") def on_dormant(self, episode_id): print(f"Converged at episode {episode_id}") Override any subset of: on_loop_start , on_loop_stop , on_episode_end(episode_id, eval_metrics) , on_improvement(snapshot) , on_plateau(episode_id, state) , on_dormant(episode_id) , on_degradation(episode_id, eval_metrics) , on_hyperparam_update(old_params, new_params) . A callback that raises inside any hook is caught and logged as a warning by LoopController - it will not crash the training run. HebbianHook and NeuromodulatorSignal (neuroevo subsystem) are also LoopCallback subclasses and can be passed alongside the above via callbacks= . Reference Full constructor parameters: Callbacks reference .

docs.text: Train an ML model (ml_core) tensor_optix.ml_core is the first-class way to train a supervised or unsupervised model with tensor-optix. The older Optimizer(model, dataset) path (see ML mode ) is built on top of the RL loop, treating each mini-batch as a fake episode. BaseMLModel / Trainer are a separate, epoch-driven contract with real classification/regression metrics and validation-based early stopping. import torch.nn as nn from tensor_optix.ml_core import TorchMLModel model = TorchMLModel( nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10)), loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss(), learning_rate=1e-3, ) history = model.fit( (X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=50, early_stopping_patience=5, checkpoint_dir="./checkpoints", ) print(history.epochs_run, history.stopped_early, history.best_epoch) print(history.val_metrics[-1].metrics) # {'accuracy': 0.94, 'f1_macro': 0.93, 'confusion_matrix_0_0': ..., ...} TorchMLModel , TFMLModel , and FlaxMLModel are provided ( from tensor_optix.ml_core import TorchMLModel, TFMLModel, FlaxMLModel ); each wraps an nn.Module / tf.keras.Model / flax.nnx.Module respectively. from flax import nnx import jax.numpy as jnp import optax from tensor_optix.ml_core import FlaxMLModel class MLP(nnx.Module): def __init__(self, din, dh, dout, rngs): self.fc1 = nnx.Linear(din, dh, rngs=rngs) self.fc2 = nnx.Linear(dh, dout, rngs=rngs) def __call__(self, x): return self.fc2(jnp.tanh(self.fc1(x))) def cross_entropy(pred, y): return jnp.mean(optax.softmax_cross_entropy_with_integer_labels(pred, y)) model = FlaxMLModel(MLP(784, 256, 10, nnx.Rngs(0)), loss_fn=cross_entropy, learning_rate=1e-3) history = model.fit((X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=50, early_stopping_patience=5) FlaxMLModel.iter_batches() only accepts a raw (X, y) array pair -- there's no Dataset/DataLoader equivalent in this codebase's JAX dependency set. Data input fit() , evaluate() , and predict() all accept either form, auto-detected: # Raw (X, y) array pair, simplest case model.fit((X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=20) # A native Dataset/DataLoader (Torch) or tf.data.Dataset (TF) model.fit(train_dataset, val_dataset, epochs=20, batch_size=64) Metrics metrics="auto" (the default) detects task type from the target dtype. Integer/class-index targets get classification metrics, float targets get regression metrics: model = TorchMLModel(net, loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss()) # metrics="auto" model = TorchMLModel(net, loss_fn=nn.MSELoss(), metrics="regression") # explicit model = TorchMLModel(net, loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss(), metrics=[my_custom_metric]) # custom callables metrics= Computed keys "classification" accuracy , precision_macro , recall_macro , f1_macro , per-class precision_<i> / recall_<i> / f1_<i> , flattened confusion_matrix_<i>_<j> "regression" mae , rmse , r2 a list of (y_true, y_pred) -> float callables one key per callable, named by __name__ Every call to evaluate() returns an MLMetrics : primary_score (higher-is-better; accuracy for classification, r2 for regression, -loss for custom metrics), loss , task_type , the full metrics dict, and epoch . This is the value checkpointing and early stopping compare against. Checkpointing and early stopping Pass checkpoint_dir to fit() to persist the best validation checkpoint via the same CheckpointRegistry the RL core uses. fit() restores the best checkpoint's weights automatically before returning, regardless of whether training ran to completion or stopped early: history = model.fit( (X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=100, early_stopping_patience=10, # stop after 10 epochs with no new best checkpoint_dir="./checkpoints", ) early_stopping_patience works even without checkpoint_dir set. "New best" is tracked independently of whether checkpoints are being persisted to disk. checkpoint_dir only controls whether that best state is saved and restorable later. Convergence/plateau detection reuses BackoffScheduler from the RL core, with defaults re-tuned for per-epoch validation curves instead of the RL defaults. Per-epoch validation curves are typically smoother and evaluated far less often than per-episode RL reward. See tensor_optix.ml_core.trainer.ML_BACKOFF_DEFAULTS for the exact values. Hyperparameter tuning If your model overrides default_param_bounds (the same mechanism MLAgent /RL agents use), Trainer activates SPSAOptimizer automatically, tuning hyperparameters once per epoch from the validation score: class MyModel(TorchMLModel): default_param_bounds = {"learning_rate": (1e-5, 1e-2), "weight_decay": (0.0, 1e-2)} TorchMLModel / TFMLModel both already set this for learning_rate / weight_decay by default. Learning-rate schedules Pass lr_schedule to fit() for a per-epoch learning-rate schedule, independent of SPSA: from tensor_optix.ml_core import StepLR, CosineAnnealingLR, WarmupLR model.fit((X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=50, lr_schedule=CosineAnnealingLR(base_lr=1e-3, epochs=50)) model.fit((X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=50, lr_schedule=StepLR(base_lr=1e-3, step_size=10, gamma=0.5)) # Linear warmup for 5 epochs, then cosine decay over the remaining 45 model.fit((X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=50, lr_schedule=WarmupLR(base_lr=1e-3, warmup_epochs=5, after=CosineAnnealingLR(base_lr=1e-3, epochs=45))) lr_schedule and SPSA are mutually exclusive for learning_rate within a single fit() call: when lr_schedule is set, Trainer drops learning_rate from the bounds it hands SPSAOptimizer for that run (a schedule and a score-driven probe both mutating the same hyperparameter every epoch would fight each other). weight_decay and any other SPSA-tunable hyperparameter are unaffected. A schedule is any callable(epoch: int) -> float , so writing a custom one is a plain function. Data augmentation def augment(X_batch, y_batch): # Torch: X_batch is a tensor; TF: X_batch is a numpy array return X_batch + torch.randn_like(X_batch) * 0.05, y_batch model.fit((X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val), epochs=20, augment=augment) augment is a callable(X_batch, y_batch) -> (X_batch, y_batch) applied to every training batch, never to validation batches. It only takes effect when train_data is a raw (X, y) array pair — if you pass a native Dataset / DataLoader / tf.data.Dataset , build augmentation into that pipeline instead (a transform on the Dataset , or .map() on the tf.data.Dataset ), which is where augmentation naturally belongs for those input forms. Pretrained backbones and transfer learning from tensor_optix.ml_core import load_pretrained_backbone, freeze_layers, unfreeze_layers import torch.nn as nn backbone = load_pretrained_backbone("resnet18", framework="torch", pretrained=True, freeze=True) model = nn.Sequential(backbone, nn.Linear(512, 10)) # resnet18's head is already stripped to nn.Identity() ml_model = TorchMLModel(model, loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss()) ml_model.fit((X_train, y_train), epochs=10) # only the new head trains while backbone is frozen unfreeze_layers(backbone) # fine-tune the whole thing afterward load_pretrained_backbone(name, framework="torch"|"tf", pretrained=True, freeze=False, input_shape=None) loads a backbone from torchvision.models (Torch) or tf.keras.applications (TF) with its classifier head removed, ready for a new head. Only a small set of common architectures is supported by name (see reference ); anything else, build it with torchvision.models / tf.keras.applications directly and pass it straight to TorchMLModel / TFMLModel . freeze_layers(model, layers=None) / unfreeze_layers(model, layers=None) work on any nn.Module or tf.keras.Model , not just backbones from load_pretrained_backbone() . layers=None freezes/unfreezes the whole model; pass submodule names (Torch, from model.named_modules() ) or layer names (TF, from layer.name ) to target specific parts. Freezing works before or after wrapping in TorchMLModel / TFMLModel -- a frozen parameter accumulates no gradient and is never updated, whether or not it was already in the optimizer's param group when fit() starts. Multi-GPU training ml_core has no first-class multi-GPU wrapper. There's no TorchMLModel(..., strategy="ddp") -style flag. Each framework's own multi-GPU mechanism is a different shape (process groups for Torch, a strategy scope for TF, explicit sharding for JAX), and wrapping all three generically behind one fit() call would hide more than it'd help. Instead, build your model with your framework's own multi-GPU mechanism before handing it to TorchMLModel / TFMLModel / FlaxMLModel — fit() / predict() / evaluate() then just run on top of it. Torch — wrap with DistributedDataParallel (multi-process, one GPU per process) before constructing TorchMLModel : import torch.distributed as dist from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl") model = MyModel().to(local_rank) model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank]) ml_model = TorchMLModel(model, loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss(), device=f"cuda:{local_rank}") ml_model.fit((X_train, y_train), epochs=50) # launch one process per GPU, e.g. via torchrun Each process gets its own TorchMLModel / Trainer / CheckpointRegistry ; only rank 0 should pass checkpoint_dir to avoid every process writing to the same files. torch.nn.DataParallel (single-process, multi-thread) also works by passing the DataParallel -wrapped module directly, but Torch itself recommends DistributedDataParallel even for single-machine use. TensorFlow — wrap the model build in tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy 's scope before constructing TFMLModel : strategy = tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy() with strategy.scope(): model = build_my_keras_model() ml_model = TFMLModel(model, loss_fn=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()) ml_model.fit((X_train, y_train), epochs=50) MirroredStrategy replicates the model across all visible GPUs on one machine and all-reduces gradients automatically; building inside its scope is what makes the model's variables mirrored. JAX/Flax — multi-GPU in JAX is explicit sharding, not a wrapper object. FlaxMLModel.train_step() calls self.model(X) and nnx.value_and_grad directly; to shard across devices, shard model 's parameters and the input batch yourself (e.g. with jax.sharding.NamedSharding / jax.jit with an explicit mesh) before calling fit() , following Flax's own multi-device guide — ml_core doesn't add anything on top of plain JAX here. None of this has been run against real multi-GPU hardware in this codebase's own test suite (CI and this repo's dev environment are CPU-only); treat it as the standard approach for each framework, not as something ml_core has verified end-to-end. docs.text: Train any PyTorch model (ML mode, legacy) Deprecated, not removed. This path treats every mini-batch as a fake RL episode, scored by an RL reward-return evaluator computing -loss , with no real classification/regression metrics. tensor_optix.ml_core ( guide ) is the first-class way to train ML models with tensor-optix - real fit() / predict() / evaluate() , real metrics, real validation-based early stopping. This path keeps working unchanged and emits a DeprecationWarning on MLAgent construction; it is not scheduled for removal. tensor-optix's loop isn't RL-specific. Pass any nn.Module and a PyTorch Dataset or DataLoader to Optimizer , and the same SPSA hyperparameter tuning, rollback-on-degradation, convergence detection, and checkpointing apply automatically - the loop treats one mini-batch as one "episode." import tensor_optix as optix import torch.nn as nn # Supervised - loss auto-detected from dataset model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10)) opt = optix.Optimizer(model, train_dataset) opt.run() # Explicit loss opt = optix.Optimizer(model, train_dataset, loss="cross_entropy") opt = optix.Optimizer(model, train_dataset, loss="mse") # Autoencoder opt = optix.Optimizer(autoencoder, train_dataset, loss="reconstruction") # VAE - model must return (reconstruction, mu, logvar) opt = optix.Optimizer(vae, train_dataset, loss="vae") # Contrastive (SimCLR) - dataset yields (view1, view2) pairs opt = optix.Optimizer(encoder, pairs_dataset, loss="contrastive") # DataLoader works too opt = optix.Optimizer(model, DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=64)) # Custom loss opt = optix.Optimizer(model, dataset, loss=nn.HuberLoss()) opt.run() Optimizer detects ML mode automatically: if agent is an nn.Module (not a BaseAgent ) and env is a Dataset / DataLoader , it builds an MLAgent wrapping your model and loss, and a DatasetPipeline wrapping your dataset, instead of an RL pipeline. Available loss= strings String Criterion Use case "auto" detected from data default "cross_entropy" CrossEntropyLoss multi-class classification "bce" BCEWithLogitsLoss binary classification "mse" MSELoss regression "mae" L1Loss regression, outlier-robust "huber" HuberLoss regression, very outlier-robust "reconstruction" MSE(output, input) autoencoders "vae" ELBO: reconstruction + KL variational autoencoders "contrastive" NT-Xent SimCLR-style contrastive learning "cosine" CosineEmbeddingLoss embedding / similarity tasks Any nn.Module or callable can be passed directly as loss= instead of a string. loss="auto" samples a few items from the dataset and infers the right loss: single-tensor items → "reconstruction" ; paired same-shape tensors → "contrastive" ; integer targets → "cross_entropy" ; float targets in {0,1} → "bce" ; float targets otherwise → "mse" . Save and load agent = optix.Optimizer(model, dataset, loss="cross_entropy") # Checkpoints written automatically to checkpoint_dir # Load back: from tensor_optix.ml import MLAgent ml_agent.load_weights("checkpoint.pt") MLAgent.is_on_policy = True - each mini-batch is independent data, so rollback on validation degradation is always safe (unlike off-policy RL agents with replay buffers). Reference MLAgent , DatasetPipeline , and the loss registry internals: ML mode reference .

docs.text: Multi-agent training (PettingZoo) tensor_optix.multi_agent drives PettingZoo environments with one ordinary tensor-optix agent per seat. Install the extra: pip install tensor-optix[torch,pettingzoo] Simultaneous-move games (Parallel API) from pettingzoo.classic import rps_v2 # any ParallelEnv from tensor_optix import make_agent from tensor_optix.multi_agent import SeatEnvView, ParallelMultiAgentPipeline, MultiAgentRunner env = rps_v2.parallel_env() env.reset(seed=0) views = {aid: SeatEnvView(env, aid) for aid in env.possible_agents} agents = {aid: make_agent(views[aid]) for aid in env.possible_agents} pipeline = ParallelMultiAgentPipeline(env, agents, window_size=256, views=views) MultiAgentRunner(pipeline, agents).run(max_windows=200) SeatEnvView gives make_agent() the single-seat observation/action spaces it needs, and one-hot encodes Discrete observations so they can feed an MLP. Turn-based games (AEC API) from pettingzoo.classic import rps_v2 from tensor_optix import make_agent from tensor_optix.multi_agent import SeatEnvView, AECMultiAgentPipeline, MultiAgentRunner env = rps_v2.env() env.reset(seed=0) views = {aid: SeatEnvView(env, aid) for aid in env.possible_agents} agents = {aid: make_agent(views[aid]) for aid in env.possible_agents} pipeline = AECMultiAgentPipeline(env, agents, window_size=400, views=views) MultiAgentRunner(pipeline, agents).run(max_windows=500) window_size here counts total env.step() calls across all seats. Rewards are credited to the action that earned them: in AEC games the result of a move (including the win/loss delivered on a seat's final turn) only becomes visible on that seat's next turn, and the pipeline writes it back onto the step that caused it - see the reference for the exact contract and its one window-boundary limitation. Action masks. Board games such as tictactoe_v3 or connect_four_v3 return a dict observation with an action_mask . The built-in agents do not apply masks; wrap the env (or the agent's act() ) so illegal moves are never selected. Convergence and checkpoints MultiAgentRunner tracks every seat separately: it scores each seat's window, checkpoints a seat whenever it beats its own best score, and detects per-seat convergence with the same trend-based BackoffScheduler the single-agent loop uses. runner = MultiAgentRunner( pipeline, agents, checkpoint_dir="./checkpoints", # one sub-directory per seat dormant_threshold=20, # flat windows before a seat counts as converged stop_when="all", # stop when every seat has converged ("any": the first) ) result = runner.run(max_windows=2000) print(result.stop_reason) # "converged" | "max_windows" | "stopped" | "pipeline_exhausted" for aid, seat in result.seats.items(): print(aid, seat.state.name, seat.best_score, seat.best_snapshot.weights_path) When the run ends each seat is restored to its best checkpoint. In a competitive game a seat's best score was earned against its opponents as they were at that moment, so the restored seats may come from different points in training - pass restore_best=False to keep the final, jointly trained weights instead (the best snapshots stay on disk). Without checkpoint_dir the runner still detects convergence and reports best scores, but saves and restores nothing. MultiAgentRunner(pipeline, agents).run(max_windows=N) therefore behaves as before, except that it can stop early once every seat has converged ( stop_on_convergence=False turns that off). Long episodes. A window is a fixed number of steps ( window_size , counted across all seats for AEC). In games whose episodes run for thousands of steps most windows contain no finished episode; those windows train the agents but are not scored, and a seat is not considered converged until it has finished min_completed_episodes_before_converged episodes (default 10). Pick a window_size large enough to hold a few episodes where you can - the trend test needs scored windows to work with. Hook into the run with a callback: class Log: def on_improvement(self, agent_id, snapshot, score): print(f"{agent_id}: new best {score:.2f}") def on_converged(self, agent_id, window_id): print(f"{agent_id} converged at window {window_id}") runner.add_callback(Log()) Hyperparameter tuning per seat Each seat is tuned online by its own optimizer, exactly as RLOptimizer tunes a single agent. It is on by default: every seat whose agent declares default_param_bounds (all built-in agents do) gets its own SPSA optimizer. After each scored window the seat's hyperparameters may be adjusted. MultiAgentRunner(pipeline, agents) # SPSA per seat (default) MultiAgentRunner(pipeline, agents, optimizer=None) # no tuning MultiAgentRunner(pipeline, agents, optimizer=lambda agent: AdaptiveOptimizer(param_bounds=agent.default_param_bounds)) result.seats[aid].hyperparams holds each seat's final hyperparameters, and on_hyperparam_update(agent_id, old, new) fires on every change. Rollback on degradation runner = MultiAgentRunner( pipeline, agents, checkpoint_dir="./checkpoints", rollback_on_degradation=True, # restore a seat's best weights if its score collapses min_consecutive_degradations=3, ) When a seat's score stays clearly below its best for several scored windows in a row, the seat is restored to its best checkpoint and keeps training. result.seats[aid].rollbacks counts how often that happened. A score also falls when an opponent gets better, so in a competitive game combine it with self-play: then only windows played against a frozen past opponent can trigger a rollback. Without self-play, enable it for cooperative games only. Self-play In a competitive game, agents that only ever face each other's current version tend to go in circles. Self-play against a pool of past snapshots fixes that. Pick the form that matches what you are training. Train every seat - each seat keeps its own policy and sometimes faces a past version of its opponent: from tensor_optix.multi_agent import SelfPlayConfig runner = MultiAgentRunner( pipeline, agents, checkpoint_dir="./checkpoints", self_play=SelfPlayConfig(snapshot_every=20, pool_size=10, opponent_prob=0.5), ) result = runner.run(max_windows=5000) print(result.pool_sizes, {a: s.frozen_windows for a, s in result.seats.items()}) A seat that is played by a snapshot for a window does not learn or get scored for that window. Train one agent for a symmetric game - the other seats become part of the environment, and the full single-agent loop drives the learner: from tensor_optix import RLOptimizer from tensor_optix.multi_agent import SelfPlayPipeline, SelfPlayConfig env = rps_v2.env() env.reset(seed=0) views = {aid: SeatEnvView(env, aid) for aid in env.possible_agents} learner = make_agent(views["player_0"]) inner = AECMultiAgentPipeline(env, {}, window_size=2048, views=views) pipeline = SelfPlayPipeline(inner, learner_seat="player_0", config=SelfPlayConfig(snapshot_every=10)) RLOptimizer(agent=learner, pipeline=pipeline, checkpoint_dir="./checkpoints").run() This form gets everything RLOptimizer offers (all optimizers, rollback on degradation, policy spawning). It requires that the opponent seats can be played by the learner's policy, i.e. the same observation and action spaces. Self-play is for competitive or mixed games; in a purely cooperative game it is the wrong tool. The defaults ( snapshot_every=20 , pool_size=10 , opponent_prob=0.5 ) are starting points, not tuned values. What you don't get Policy spawning is not part of MultiAgentRunner (use SelfPlayPipeline + RLOptimizer when one learner is enough). One policy shared across seats, league training, and centralized critics are out of scope.

docs.text: Build a neuroevo agent pip install tensor-optix[neuroevo] The neuroevo subsystem represents a policy as a NeuronGraph : a mutable directed graph of heterogeneous scalar neurons (point, GRU, LSTM, trainable-GRU, trainable-LSTM) connected by variable-delay edges. A TopologyController runs as a loop callback and mutates this graph live during training - growing capacity when the existing network is saturated, pruning dead neurons and edges, and merging redundant ones. Quickest path: make_agent from tensor_optix import make_agent import gymnasium as gym env = gym.make("LunarLanderContinuous-v3") agent = make_agent(env, neuroevo=True) agent = make_agent("PPO", env, neuroevo=True, graph_hidden=16, hebbian_lr=1e-3) # Feature-extractor mode: NeuronGraph -> features concatenated to obs, fed into SAC agent = make_agent("SAC", env, neuroevo=True, neuroevo_mode="feature_extractor") neuroevo_mode controls how the graph is used: "policy" (default) - the graph is the policy, wrapped as GraphAgent (PPO-based). "feature_extractor" - the graph runs in parallel as a feature extractor; its output is concatenated with the raw observation before SAC's actor/critic networks. SAC handles exploration and replay; the graph adds adaptive temporal features via GRU + LSTM neurons with Hebbian learning. Neuroevo options on make_agent : graph_in (default min(obs_dim, 16) ), graph_hidden (default 8), graph_out (default act_dim + 1 ), hebbian_lr , hebbian_decay , grow_cooldown . Neuroevo only supports flat 1-D Box observation spaces. NeuronGraph 's input neurons are 1:1 with flattened observation scalars, so images and Dict observations (supported in the standard, non-neuroevo path via tensor_optix.encoders ) aren't supported here. make_agent(neuroevo=True) raises NotImplementedError immediately if the observation space isn't flat Box . Building a graph manually from tensor_optix.neuroevo import NeuronGraph, GraphAgent, GRUNeuron, LSTMNeuron graph = NeuronGraph() for _ in range(4): graph.add_neuron(role="input", activation="linear") for _ in range(8): graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", activation="tanh") # or: graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", neuron=GRUNeuron()) # or: graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", neuron=LSTMNeuron()) graph.add_neuron(role="output", activation="linear") # last output neuron is the value head graph.add_edge(src_id, dst_id, weight=0.0, delay=0) # feedforward (d=0) graph.add_edge(src_id, dst_id, weight=0.0, delay=1) # recurrent (d>=1, reads from history buffer) agent = GraphAgent(graph, obs_dim=4, n_actions=2) All edges initialize at weight=0.0 , which is function-preserving at insertion time - this is the same Net2Net-style principle behind every topology operation (see Topology operations ). Neuron types Type Hidden state Gradient through state Neuron None (point neuron) N/A GRUNeuron Scalar h, detached No LSTMNeuron Scalar h and c, detached No TrainableGRUNeuron Scalar h, not detached Yes, up to chunk_len steps TrainableLSTMNeuron Scalar h and c, not detached Yes, up to chunk_len steps All types implement the same protocol ( step() , importance() , can_merge_with() , make_relay() , split_copy() ) - NeuronGraph and TopologyController are type-blind. Trainable recurrent neurons TrainableGRUNeuron / TrainableLSTMNeuron set is_recurrent = True . RecurrentGraphAgent detects this and switches from shuffled-minibatch PPO to sequential chunk training with truncated BPTT: from tensor_optix.neuroevo import TrainableGRUNeuron, TrainableLSTMNeuron, RecurrentGraphAgent from tensor_optix.core.types import HyperparamSet graph = NeuronGraph() # ... input and output neurons ... graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", neuron=TrainableGRUNeuron()) graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", neuron=TrainableLSTMNeuron()) agent = RecurrentGraphAgent( graph, obs_dim=4, n_actions=2, hyperparams=HyperparamSet(params={"chunk_len": 64}), ) # Falls back to standard shuffled-minibatch PPO if no recurrent neurons are present The topology controller from tensor_optix.neuroevo import TopologyController controller = TopologyController.for_graph( graph=graph, scheduler=opt._scheduler, grow_grad_threshold=0.7, # fraction of hidden neurons with |grad| > eps required to grow prune_neuron_threshold=1e-4, # importance score below this -> prune candidate prune_edge_threshold=1e-3, # |weight| below this for prune_edge_patience episodes -> prune merge_similarity_threshold=0.95, # Pearson correlation threshold for merge ) opt.add_callback(controller) opt.run() A grow operation fires only when all three statistical signals agree: Improvement test - the score slope is not significantly positive (a corrected t-test) - i.e. gradient updates have stalled. Structure test - score residuals show significant lag-1 autocorrelation - i.e. there's unexplained structure the model isn't capturing. Capacity test - gradient utilization across hidden neurons exceeds grow_grad_threshold - i.e. existing neurons are saturated, not idle. For multi-region graphs, use TopologyController.for_brain(brain, scheduler=...) - each region gets independent signal buffers and cooldown timers, so a saturated encoder region can grow without triggering growth elsewhere. Save and load Topology is saved alongside weights, so a checkpoint fully reconstructs the graph on load - no manual topology bookkeeping: agent.save_weights("checkpoint.pt") agent2 = make_agent(env, neuroevo=True) agent2.load_weights("checkpoint.pt") # Or skip constructing an agent entirely agent3 = GraphAgent.from_checkpoint("checkpoint.pt") agent3.act(obs) Rollback on degradation uses the same path - when the loop restores a best checkpoint, the topology at the time of that checkpoint is fully restored, even if the graph has grown or been pruned since. BrainNetwork: composing multiple regions from tensor_optix.neuroevo import BrainNetwork, TopologyController brain = BrainNetwork() brain.add_region("sensory", sensory_graph) brain.add_region("memory", memory_graph) brain.add_region("executive", executive_graph) brain.add_pathway("sensory", "memory", n_connections=8, delay=1) brain.add_pathway("memory", "executive", n_connections=8, delay=0) controller = TopologyController.for_brain(brain, scheduler=opt._scheduler) Inter-region edges are learnable parameters; when a neuron is pruned from a region, BrainNetwork automatically removes all inter-region edges referencing it. Hebbian learning from tensor_optix.neuroevo import HebbianHook hook = HebbianHook(graph, hebbian_lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4) for step in episode: action = agent.act(obs) hook.record() obs, reward, done, _ = env.step(action) agent.learn(episode_data) hook.apply() hook.reset() HebbianHook is a LoopCallback - pass it directly via callbacks= and it wires itself automatically (it records after every act() and applies the update after each learn() ; don't call record() yourself in that case). Use HebbianHook.from_brain(brain, ...) for BrainNetwork graphs. Neuromodulation from tensor_optix.neuroevo import NeuromodulatorSignal from tensor_optix.core import RegimeDetector signal = NeuromodulatorSignal( detector=RegimeDetector(), hebbian_hook=hook, # optional agent=agent, # optional - modulates entropy_coef topology_controller=tc, # optional - modulates grow/prune thresholds ) opt = Optimizer(agent, env, callbacks=[hook, signal]) opt.run() NeuromodulatorSignal maps a RegimeDetector classification (trending / ranging / volatile) to coordinated parameter changes: trending → lower Hebbian lr and entropy (consolidate); ranging → raise Hebbian lr, lower grow threshold (explore structure); volatile → lower Hebbian lr, raise entropy (cautious plasticity). Dale's Law # clamp mode (default): outgoing weights clamped post-step graph = NeuronGraph(dale_mode="clamp") graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", activation="relu", cell_type="excitatory") # weights >= 0 graph.add_neuron(role="hidden", activation="tanh", cell_type="inhibitory") # weights <= 0 # softplus mode: raw parameter theta, effective weight = softplus(theta) * sign # gradient-safe, no dead zone at the clamp boundary graph = NeuronGraph(dale_mode="softplus") w = graph.effective_weight(edge_id) # reads post-softplus value Compiled forward NeuronGraph runs eager by default - _raw_forward mutates Python-side neuron state, which torch.compile can't safely trace without replaying side effects. If your topology is static and you manage neuron state externally, opt in: graph.compile_forward() # one-time call; re-call after any topology mutation TopologyController calls graph.invalidate_compile() automatically after every grow/prune/merge. If you mutate the graph directly outside the controller, call it yourself. Reference Full class and function documentation: Neuroevo reference . Things to know make_agent(env, neuroevo=True) attaches its HebbianHook and TopologyController as agent._neuroevo_callbacks ; Optimizer wires them into the loop automatically. With RLOptimizer , pass them yourself: callbacks=agent._neuroevo_callbacks . In neuroevo_mode="feature_extractor" the graph is a recurrent feature extractor in front of SAC. Checkpoints contain the SAC networks and the graph (topology + weights) and the fixed random projection, so a restored agent reproduces the same features. The features the policy acted on are cached and reused by learn() . Restoring a checkpoint (rollback, best-weight restore at the end of run() ) rebuilds the graph in place - callbacks keep operating on the live graph.
